loreChunks.title: Kathmandu's Ganesh of Beginnings
loreChunks.text: Ashok Binayak, also called Maru Ganesh after the Maru neighbourhood, is a small but immensely popular Ganesh shrine at the corner of Kasthamandap, at the south-western entrance to Kathmandu Durbar Square. Its name is traditionally linked to an ashoka tree that once grew here. The shrine is often named among the principal Ganesh temples of the Kathmandu Valley, though lists of the valley's foremost Ganesh shrines differ between traditions. Its founding date has not been established in Saalik's sources, but its position beside the pavilion that gave Kathmandu its name places it at the historic heart of the city, at the meeting of old trade routes. For centuries Kathmandu residents have stopped here before journeys and new ventures, and the shrine's importance is out of all proportion to its tiny size. It is one of the busiest places of worship in the old city.

loreChunks.title: A Small Gilded Shrine
loreChunks.text: Ashok Binayak is a compact shrine with a gilded roof and a richly decorated front, set at the corner of the Kasthamandap platform. Its small size means that devotees worship from the street, standing before the image to make offerings, ring the bell and receive a tika of red powder. The gilded metalwork of the roof and the frame catches the morning light, and the shrine is almost always surrounded by worshippers. Its placement at Maru, where streets converge, makes it a natural stopping point for people passing through the old city on foot or by motorbike. The shrine's architecture is modest, but its decoration reflects the generosity of devotees over the centuries, who have donated metal ornaments and offerings. Field collectors are asked to photograph the shrine early in the morning, before the crowds, to record its gilded details clearly.

loreChunks.title: The Remover of Obstacles
loreChunks.text: Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati, is the god of beginnings and the remover of obstacles, worshipped before any important undertaking. His image at Ashok Binayak is covered in red powder and offerings, so that its features are often hidden beneath layers of devotion. His vehicle, the shrew, symbolises the ability to overcome any obstacle, however small or hidden, and his elephant head stands for wisdom. In the Newar tradition, Ganesh is worshipped first in every ritual, and every neighbourhood has its own Ganesh shrine. Ashok Binayak's location at the entrance to the royal square suggests that he guarded the threshold of the city's sacred centre, ensuring that all who entered did so under his protection. For visitors, the shrine offers a vivid example of everyday devotion in the city, where a quick prayer to Ganesh begins the day.

loreChunks.title: A Prayer on the Way to Work
loreChunks.text: From dawn until late at night, Ashok Binayak receives a constant stream of devotees: commuters on their way to work, families preparing for weddings, students before examinations and travellers before long journeys. Many touch the shrine, ring the bell and receive a tika in a matter of seconds, while others linger to make more elaborate offerings. Tuesdays, sacred to Ganesh in Nepal, are especially busy, and the festival of Ganesh Chaturthi brings large crowds. New vehicles are sometimes brought to be blessed by priests nearby. The shrine's priests and attendants keep the offerings flowing, and the area around it is lined with sellers of flowers and sweets. Visitors are welcome to observe and may receive a tika if they wish. The shrine is a perfect place to begin a walk through Durbar Square, just as Kathmandu residents begin their own journeys here.

loreChunks.title: Survival Beside a Collapsed Neighbour
loreChunks.text: When Kasthamandap collapsed in the 2015 earthquake, the small Ashok Binayak shrine at its corner survived, and worshippers continued to visit it amid the rubble, a scene that became a symbol of resilience for many residents. The shrine required inspection and minor repair, and its surroundings were transformed during the years of Kasthamandap's reconstruction. The heavy daily use of the shrine wears its metalwork and surroundings, and offerings must be cleared regularly. Its gilded elements require periodic cleaning and regilding, coordinated with the priests. The shrine's conservation is closely linked with that of Kasthamandap and the Maru area, which have been the focus of community-led rebuilding. Saalik's field collectors are asked to photograph the shrine before the morning crowds, recording its gilded details and its relationship to the rebuilt pavilion, so that changes can be tracked over time.

audioHook.script: Before you leave Durbar Square, watch this tiny golden shrine for a minute. Commuters on motorbikes slow down, students touch the step, a family with a new car waits for a blessing. This is Ashok Binayak, also called Maru Ganesh, the elephant-headed remover of obstacles, and Kathmandu residents have stopped here before journeys, exams and weddings for centuries. Its name is said to come from an ashoka tree that once grew on this spot. When the great wooden Kasthamandap beside it collapsed in the 2015 earthquake, this little shrine survived, and people kept praying here amid the rubble. You have come full circle to where the walk began. Ring the bell if you like, and ask Ganesh to bless your next journey. Book a verified local storyteller nearby and let a guide plan your next walk in the valley.
